    toc: true

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE)
library(infer)
data("yrbss", package = "openintro")
set.seed(1234)
alpha <- 0.05
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * x)
boot_summary <- function(event, outcome) {
  d <- data.frame(response = ifelse(event, "yes", "no"))
  d <- d[!is.na(d$response), , drop = FALSE]
  ci <- d |>
    specify(response = response, success = "yes") |>
    generate(reps = 5000, type = "bootstrap") |>
    calculate(stat = "prop") |>
    get_confidence_interval(level = 0.95)
  data.frame(outcome, n = nrow(d), estimate = mean(d$response == "yes"),
             lower = ci[[1]], upper = ci[[2]],
             margin = (ci[[2]] - ci[[1]]) / 2)
}
```

## 1. Texting while driving

```{r}
table(yrbss$text_while_driving_30d, useNA = "ifany")
```

Each count corresponds to a reported category. Missing responses are listed
separately from the reported categories.

## 2–3. Daily texting among students who never wear a helmet

```{r}
no_helmet <- subset(yrbss, helmet_12m == "never")
text_ci <- boot_summary(no_helmet$text_while_driving_30d == "30",
                        "Daily texting among non-helmet wearers")
text_ci
```

**2.** The conditional sample proportion is `r pct(text_ci$estimate)`, using
students who answered the texting question and said they never wear a helmet.

**3.** The approximate 95% margin of error is
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * text_ci$margin)` percentage points, using half the
width of the bootstrap percentile interval. The interval runs from
`r pct(text_ci$lower)` to `r pct(text_ci$upper)`.

## 4. Two other categorical outcomes

```{r}
active_ci <- boot_summary(yrbss$physically_active_7d == 7,
                          "Physically active on all seven days")
sleep_ci <- boot_summary(yrbss$school_night_hours_sleep == "10+",
                         "Ten or more hours of school-night sleep")
rbind(active_ci, sleep_ci)
```

For daily physical activity, the 95% interval is `r pct(active_ci$lower)` to
`r pct(active_ci$upper)`, with an approximate margin of
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * active_ci$margin)` percentage points. For reporting
at least ten hours of school-night sleep, the interval is
`r pct(sleep_ci$lower)` to `r pct(sleep_ci$upper)`, with a margin of
`r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * sleep_ci$margin)` percentage points. These are
unweighted estimates for the corresponding student proportions under the
lab's independent-sampling approximation.

## 5. Margin of error versus population proportion

```{r}
p <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01)
margin <- function(p, n) qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
plot(p, margin(p, 1000), type = "l", xlab = "Population proportion",
     ylab = "95% margin of error", main = "Fixed sample size of 1,000")
abline(v = 0.5, lty = 2)
```

The margin of error increases to a maximum at 0.50 and then decreases
symmetrically, since the product of p and 1 minus p is greatest there.

## 6–8. Sampling distributions

```{r}
sim_prop <- function(n, p) rbinom(5000, n, p) / n
settings <- data.frame(n = c(300, 300, 300, 30, 1000),
                       p = c(0.1, 0.01, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1))
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(settings))) {
  x <- sim_prop(settings$n[i], settings$p[i])
  hist(x, breaks = 15, xlab = "Sample proportion",
       main = paste("n =", settings$n[i], "| p =", settings$p[i]))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
transform(settings, standard_error = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n))
```

**6.** With n = 300 and p = 0.10 the center is 0.10, the standard error
is about 0.0173 and the shape is roughly bell-shaped with some right skew.

**7.** Holding n fixed, the center tracks p. Spread increases toward p = 0.5.
Near 0 or 1 the distribution has less spread and can be visibly skewed.

**8.** Holding p fixed, larger samples tighten the distribution around p
and generally make its shape more nearly normal.

## 9. Sleep and daily strength training

Let p1 and p2 be the proportions who strength train every day among students
reporting 10+ hours and under 10 hours of sleep, respectively.
Test H0: p1 = p2 versus HA: p1 > p2 at alpha = 0.05.

```{r}
sleep_train <- with(yrbss, table(
  sleep = factor(ifelse(school_night_hours_sleep == "10+", "10+", "under 10"),
                 levels = c("10+", "under 10")),
  training = factor(ifelse(strength_training_7d == 7, "daily", "other"),
                    levels = c("daily", "other"))))
sleep_train
training_test <- if (all(sleep_train >= 10)) {
  prop.test(sleep_train, alternative = "greater", correct = FALSE)
} else {
  fisher.test(sleep_train, alternative = "greater")
}
training_test
two_sided_ci <- if (training_test$p.value < alpha && all(sleep_train >= 10)) {
  prop.test(sleep_train, correct = FALSE)$conf.int
}
if (!is.null(two_sided_ci)) two_sided_ci
```

Each student contributes to one cell, and the groups are disjoint. The table
checks the success and failure counts. The two-proportion approximation is used
when all four counts are at least ten, with an exact test available otherwise.
The dataset does not supply school cluster or survey weight information for
the lab calculation, so this analysis uses the independent-student approximation.
The one-sided p-value is `r format.pval(training_test$p.value, digits = 3)`.
At 0.05 there is `r if (training_test$p.value < alpha) "evidence" else "insufficient evidence"`
that the 10+ hour group is more likely to strength train every day.
`r if (!is.null(two_sided_ci)) paste("The two-sided 95% interval for the difference is", paste(pct(two_sided_ci), collapse = " to "), "(10+ hours minus under 10 hours).") else ""`

## 10. Type I error

At a 0.05 significance level, the nominal probability of detecting a difference
when the null hypothesis is true is 5%.

## 11. Sample size for weekly service attendance

```{r}
ceiling(qnorm(0.975)^2 * 0.5 * (1 - 0.5) / 0.01^2)
```

Use p = 0.5 for the most conservative calculation. A simple random sample
of at least 9,604 residents meets the stated margin-of-error target.
